title: Decision-making at the crime scene: A scoping literature review on the cognitive aspects of crime scene examination and the influence of rapid testing

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Decision-making at the crime scene: A scoping literature review on the cognitive aspects of crime scene examination and the influence of rapid testing》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p0010】Technological advances have led to techniques that allow for rapid on-site analysis of forensic traces (see, for example, [1], [2], [3], [4]). In time, these rapid techniques may become available to crime scene investigators, which would allow them to already use the results of rapid analyses during their examination of the crime scene. This is in stark contrast to the current situation where the results of conventional analyses typically only become available after traces have been collected and submitted to a laboratory. Although innovations have also reduced the time laboratories need to produce results, in the Netherlands only highly urgent biological traces suitable for DNA analysis can be analysed and compared with the DNA database within hours. For most other DNA-bearing traces, this typically takes three days, provided that the traces are already sampled by the police and immediately submitted to the laboratory [5]. Similarly, it takes two working days for the results of toxicological analyses to become available [6]. Because conventional trace analysis typically takes days, except for highly urgent traces, its outcomes often cannot be used to inform decision-making at the crime scene. As a result, decisions made during the crime scene examination are based on limited information. The rapid nature of new techniques may, to some extent, change this by providing additional information at an early stage, helping investigators better understand what may have happened and which traces may warrant collection. Although rapid testing may, accordingly, change how crime scenes are examined, its use is likely to interact with existing practices. Current practices inform search strategies and will continue to influence where crime scene investigators initially search for traces and which traces become available for rapid analysis. Within this process, rapid tests may support the detection or visualisation of traces, thereby, influencing which traces are noticed and which information becomes available. Moreover, rapid tests that provide additional information about the traces can further influence which information is available and how information is interpreted. This may, in turn, influence where crime scene investigators search for additional traces and which traces they decide to collect and analyse. Rapid testing may therefore create a continuous feedback loop during crime scene examination, whereby preliminary results inform subsequent search and recovery activities, enabling investigators to target and rapidly analyse the most relevant traces. As the influence of rapid testing may thus become intertwined with current practices of crime scene examination and decision-making, understanding the interaction between current practices and the use of rapid tests is essential to anticipate consequences of implementation in practice. Although practical implementation may depend on other factors as well, such as operational or organisational constraints and the quality of the rapid test, the cognitive processes underlying crime scene examination warrant particular attention. Rapid testing introduces new information into an examination that is already shaped by investigators’ expectations, attention, interpretations, and decisions. How this new information is noticed, interpreted, and incorporated into subsequent decisions may therefore influence how crime scenes are searched, which traces are recognised as relevant, and which traces are selected for further examination. It is therefore imperative to understand how crime scene investigators currently find, recognise, collect, and analyse traces and to explore how the availability and use of rapid tests may influence this, in order to identify which questions need to be answered before rapid testing can be implemented. We therefore first discuss the phases of crime scene examinations and the cognitive aspects and decision-making that play a role in these examinations, before turning to the empirical literature on how crime scene investigators examine crime scenes and how rapid testing appears to influence these processes.

【Finding traces · p0045】At the crime scene, the forensic investigation mainly consists of searching for and collecting traces. Although the ISO-norms and ENFSI-guidelines describe this process, they provide limited practical guidance on how traces should be identified and prioritised. By largely leaving these decisions unaddressed, these guidelines seem to either implicitly frame trace detection as a neutral and objective process or seem to remain at a high abstraction level resulting in limited practical guidance. After all, it has long been established that perception is selective and shaped by observers’ expectations, goals and prior knowledge and attentional resources (see Refs. [23], [24] for a review). An experiment showed, for instance, that 20 out of 24 experienced radiologists failed to notice a gorilla in a lung-nodule detection task while examining chest CT-scans, even though the gorilla was 48 times larger than the average nodule and eye-tracking data showed that most radiologists looked directly at its location [25]. Drew et al. hypothesised that the radiologists may have missed the gorilla because it did not resemble the lung nodules they were searching for. This study demonstrates that even experts can fail to notice abnormal stimuli that they looked at directly. Noticing stimuli or traces, thus, requires more than simply looking everywhere. This issue is further exacerbated by the increasing ability to collect and analyse smaller traces [26], including traces that are not visible to the naked eye. Visual cues alone are therefore insufficient to guide the search for traces. Instead, crime scene investigators must actively search for them, for example by applying and subsequently removing powder to a surface to reveal potential fingermarks [27], or blindly sample for invisible traces like touch DNA or saliva. Because not every surface can be powdered or sampled, investigators must identify and prioritise specific areas for examination rather than rely solely on systematic search patterns.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Decision-making at the crime scene: A scoping literature review on the cognitive aspects of crime scene examination and the influence of rapid testing》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Methods · p0070】This literature review sought to investigate the cognitive processes underlying decision-making in crime scene investigations and to assess the potential impact of rapid testing on those processes. Given the broad nature of this topic, we used a scoping approach to the search for and selection of studies with broad search terms and inclusion criteria. However, decision-making processes at the crime scene have received limited attention in the literature. The review, therefore, focuses on studies addressing the search for, interpretation, collection, and analysis of traces, and the use and influence of rapid tests. For articles to be included, they had to (1) explicitly report how people in practice make or would make decisions regarding the approach of the crime scene examination (e.g., the search strategy), decisions regarding traces and their interpretation and (rapid) analysis, decisions regarding the overall interpretation of the crime scene; (2) report original empirical findings; (3) be written in English or Dutch; and (4) be accessible through open access or an institutional subscription. Both peer-reviewed or non-peer-reviewed articles were ultimately eligible for inclusion. Articles were excluded if they: (1) described purely conceptual or theoretical models of crime scene examination without presenting original empirical findings; (2) concerned processes occurring after completion of the crime scene examination that do not affect decisions made at the crime scene or the potential use of rapid tests; and (3) focused exclusively on technical aspects, such as preferences for a particular collection method, which fell outside the scope of this review. Trace analysis was retained within the scope, because the anticipated analysis of traces may influence decision-making at the crime scene (p. 21) [32], and because the decision to analyse a trace may reflect future decision-making regarding the use of rapid tests. Studies published up until the date of retrieval were eligible for inclusion. In addition, relevant studies published after this date were included if they came to the authors’ attention.

【Methods · p0075】The identification of relevant literature consisted of several steps, starting with using keywords for decision-making2 and for crime scene examination3 to search the Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, APA PsycINFO, International Bibliography of the Social Sciences, and Criminal Justice Abstracts (see Appendix A for the search queries and number of results). As this review focuses on the cognitive aspects of crime scene examination, databases were selected that include general, psychological and criminological literature and that were accessible through institutional subscriptions. The databases were searched on October 8, 2025, resulting in only English-language articles. In Scopus, English was applied as an explicit filter, because no Dutch-language results were identified, whereas several articles in other languages could be excluded. The Scopus search results were also limited to journal articles, as the search initially focused on identifying peer-reviewed articles reporting original results. These searches resulted in 911 records. As an initial screening indicated that relatively few records were relevant, the inclusion criteria were broadened to also include non-peer reviewed articles. Google Scholar was therefore searched on October 27, 2025, using the same keyword combinations as in the other database searches. A second Google Scholar search was conducted on October 31, 2025, using the term “mock crime scene” and combinations of keywords related to crime scene examination and trace interpretation.4 In addition, Scopus was searched again on August 25, 2026, with filters limiting the search results to conference papers, book chapters, and books. Ultimately, all search results from Scopus that may include original results were included. This led to a combined total of 1157 articles that were extracted, either through functionality provided by the database or through using reference manager Zotero (version 7.0.27), and combined into a single Excel file. To remove duplicates, all titles were converted to lowercase to harmonize formatting, and a new variable was created containing the DOI or, if no DOI was associated with the entry, the row number. Excel's functionality was then used to remove duplicates based on the lowercase titles and the new variable, resulting in 789 unique articles. These unique articles were manually screened based on their titles and abstracts, resulting in 79 potentially relevant articles.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Decision-making at the crime scene: A scoping literature review on the cognitive aspects of crime scene examination and the influence of rapid testing》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【The interpretation of the crime scene at the conclusion of the examination · p0180】The final interpretation of the crime scene, after the search for and collection of traces has been completed, strongly depends on the earlier phases and decision steps, as they determine which information is available. This already starts before the crime scene is examined, as prior information may already influence expectations and the traces that are found. The experiment performed by Van den Eeden et al. [38], as discussed in 3.1, demonstrates that prior information pertaining to the cause of death can influence not only the first impression but also the most likely scenario after the crime scene has been processed. Although processing the crime scene led to more correct decisions, participants in the suicide condition were less likely than expected to correctly interpret the crime scene as a murder. This difference was, however, not significant [38]. A more recent study comparing English, Norwegian, and Swedish crime scene investigators with English laypersons similarly found that experienced crime scene investigators who received prior information indicating a homicide were more likely to judge the scene as a homicide than those that received prior information indicating a suicide, although the difference was again not statistically significant. The impressions and confidence judgements from English laypersons were, however, significantly influenced in line with the prior information [59]. The experiment conducted by De Roo et al. [44] where crime scene examiners were provided a behavioural report from investigative psychologists further suggests that bias may influence the final interpretation of a crime scene. Crime scene investigators who incorrectly interpreted the crime scene as that of a suicide were nevertheless very confident in their assessment and claimed not to need the additional information. As a result, none of those crime scene investigators changed their interpretation, even though the behavioural report could have led them to the correct decision as the investigative psychologists were significantly more likely to interpret the crime scene as that of a domestic homicide [44]. Regardless of bias, it appears that experts may be better at interpreting crime scenes than novices [48].

【The influence of rapid testing on the interpretation of the crime scene at the conclusion of the examination · p0190】Nevertheless, the fact that not all crime scene investigators changed their scenario in light of the new information, suggests that earlier beliefs may influence the interpretation of rapid test results. This may suggest that information is primarily integrated if the results align with the beliefs of the investigator [60]. Similarly, rapid identification results may result in crime scene investigators giving undue weight to traces, where traces that lead to an identification were considered to be more important than traces in a similar context that did not result in an identification [66]. This effect was only found among English and not Dutch crime scene investigators, which may be explained by a difference in the aim of the investigation. English crime scene investigators may be more focused on efficiently identifying suspects, while Dutch crime scene investigators may be more focused on reconstructing events [53]. It is therefore important to further study how rapid test results can best be integrated into scenario construction and how the influence of bias in this regard can be minimized.

sections.title: 复现线索
sections.text:
《Decision-making at the crime scene: A scoping literature review on the cognitive aspects of crime scene examination and the influence of rapid testing》：复现时可直接核对的数据、软件或实现线索。

【Bias prevention · p0210】Rather than initially withholding information from crime scene investigators, another approach emphasizes the consideration of alternative scenarios (see, for example, [16], [69], [70], [71], [72], [73]). This approach posits that findings should be evaluated by assessing how well they discriminate between plausible alternative scenarios. The NFI collaborates with law enforcement and academic partners to further develop this approach into practical steps that crime scene investigators can follow [74]. Their scenario-driven method for examining crime scenes aims not only to minimise the influence of cognitive biases but also to assist crime scene investigators in finding traces. While assessing the crime scene, investigators record their observations and use these observations to formulate scenarios about what might have happened. By identifying points of interests and key questions, crime scene investigators are guided in which topics warrant the development of scenes, or possible sequences of events. Crime scene investigators can then reason about the traces they would expect (not) to find if a given scene were accurate (see for a more detailed explanation [75]). For example, if investigators observe blood on a broken window, they might hypothesise that this was caused by the perpetrator being injured while breaking in. This could then prompt them to search for traces related to tending to that injury, such as in the bathroom. This is an iterative process, since any new traces found in subsequent searches can refine existing scenarios, lead to the creation of new scenes, and result in the detection of other traces. Considering alternative scenarios or scenes, while recording and explicating the observations and information on which these scenes are based, may make investigators realise that their beliefs about what happened could be mistaken and prompt them to search for traces that do not fit those beliefs. Additionally, this approach might not only combat the undue influence of bias, but also provide practical guidance to the use of rapid testing as the results could benefit the investigation if they can help discriminate between possible scenarios.
